Control Number - 59142

                                      PROJECT NO. 59142

REVIEW OF ERCOT'S                                    §     PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
INTERCONNECTION PROCESSES FOR                        §
LARGELOADS                                           §             OF TEXAS


 SYNERGEN'S REQUEST FOR GOOD CAUSE EXCEPTION RELATING TO BATCH
                   ZERO ELIGIBILITY DEADLINES

        Synergen Green Energy, Inc. ("Synergen"), an Interconnecting Large Load Entity
("ILLE") seeking ERCOT Batch Zero inclusion for its green ammonia production facility (the
"Project"), submits this request to the Public Utility Commission of Texas ("PUCT" or
"Commission"). Synergen respectfully requests that the Commission grant this good cause
exception from the Batch Zero eligibility deadlines in Planning Guide §§ 9.2.1.1 and 9.2.1.2 and
direct ERCOT to include the Proj ect in the Batch Zero process.

        The Commission has broad authority under 16 TAC § 25.3(b) to grant good cause
exceptions to its rules, and ERCOT must carry out its duties under applicable ERCOT rules,
including the Planning Guide, as required by 16 TAC § 25.361(b)(16). The requested exception is
consistent with that authority and with the substantive legal standards governing large-load
interconnection.

                                EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

         Synergen respectfully requests that the Commission grant a good cause exception
authorizing ERCOT to include Synergen' s Project, an approximately 300 MW green ammonia
production facility in Calhoun County, in the Batch Zero process, notwithstanding Synergen' s
inability to meet the Batch Zero eligibility deadlines established by Planning Guide Revision
Request ("PGRR") 145. PGRR 145 was approved on June 18, 2026 and took effect just twenty-
three days later, on July 11, 2026, imposing new eligibility deadlines of July 10 and July 24, 2026
that Synergen, a small-medium developer with no prior experience in the ERCOT interconnection
process, was generally unaware of and unable to meet.

        Synergen has already invested approximately $30.5 million in the Project' s permitting,
engineering, and site development, consistent with a conventional, good-faith development path.
The financial security requirement was imposed in part as a mechanism of validating "real" or
"actual" large load projects. In comparison to the investment of $30.5 Million already made by
Synergen, the security deposit would have been $15 million.

       Absent an exception, the Project would be barred from Initial Energization until an
undefined future interconnection study process, stranding Synergen's investment and the jobs and
tax revenue the Project would bring to Calhoun County. Good cause exists because PGRR 145's



                                                 1
 compressed implementation left Synergen unable to comply with deadlines it reasonably did not
anticipate; because industrial large loads should not be collateral to the onslaught of large
computational loads ("LCLs") seeking energization in the State, and because Synergen is prepared
to structure any required financial security to reflect the realities of industrial proj ect finance.
Synergen accordingly requests that the Commission direct ERCOT to include the Project in Batch
Zero and treat the applicable eligibility deadlines as satisfied while this request is pending.



                                I.      PROJECT BACKGROUND

         Synergen is developing a green ammonia production facility -not a data center - in the
South Texas Electric Cooperative, Inc. ("STEC") service territory in south Texas. Ammonia is a
critical and highly versatile industrial product used in agriculture, power generation, cold storage
refrigeration, shipping fuel, and energy storage, and is produced through an electrochemical
process that requires large-scale electric service. The Project represents a significant investment in
Texas's industrial base and clean energy economy.

       Work on the Proj ect has already commenced. To date, Synergen has invested
approximately $30.5 million in permitting studies, engineering, environmental assessments,
groundwater assessments, equipment procurement, and site preparation. These investments are
substantial , largely irreversible , and were undertaken in reasonable reliance on the establishedload
interconnection framework then in effect.

        The Project is located on a 170.4-acre site in Calhoun County under Synergen's control,
with an additional five-acre leased parcel at the Port of Calhoun for ammonia storage and marine
loading. As designed, the facility is capable of producing approximately 219,000 metric tons of
clean ammonia annually. The Project requires 300 MW of grid capacity, which will ultimately be
powered by Synergen' s investments in a 290 MW behind the meter solar facility and 600 MW of
Texas sourced wind generation through a virtual Power Purchase Agreement ("VPPA"). Synergen
does not intend to draw solely from the ERCOT grid, but rather plans to bring its own substantial
and contracted generation capacity for the Proj ect. Synergen' s approach is consistent with the
"bring-your-own-generation" pathways ERCOT has separately recognized as reducing net
transmission burden and improving system resource adequacy.

        Synergen first engaged STEC regarding the Proj ect' s interconnection in July of 2024, and
the parties have worked continuously together since that time - including through Synergen
contracting with STEC to perform a Load Study and ERCOT System Impact Study in August
2025, for which Synergen paid STEC an upfront $200,000 fee. Construction of the Project is
expected to begin in the first quarter of 2027 with Start-Up, in the first quarter of 2029.

       The Project is expected to create approximately 60 permanent, full-time high-paying jobs
at Start-Up and approximately 150 construction jobs at peak. Total project expenditures are


                                                  2
 estimated at approximately $568 million, that would substantially expand the local tax base
supporting Calhoun County, Calhoun ISD, the Calhoun County Groundwater Conservation
District, and the Calhoun Port Authority, taxing jurisdictions in a rural county where new industrial
investment, jobs, and tax revenue support essential local services, including public schools and the
county hospital district. If the Project cannot proceed on a commercially viable timeline because
of exclusion from Batch Zero, the region would lose not only these jobs and this tax base, but the
broader economic activity that a project of this scale would generate.


         II.      GOOD CAUSE EXISTS FOR THE REQUESTED EXCEPTION

    A. ERCOT's Batch Zero Process Is a Fundamental Departure from Prior
       Interconnection Practice That Connected Loads in a Sustainable and
       Sequenced Manner.
        PGRR 145 was adopted on an accelerated schedule: the Commission approved it on June
 18, 2026, and it became effective only twenty-three days later, on July 11, 2026. PGRR 145
imposed Batch Zero ILLE eligibility deadlines of July 10, 2026 (for dynamic data submissions
and certain attestations) and July 24, 2026 (for TSP submissions of eligibility information,
financial security, attestations, and disclosures). The Batch Zero process created by PGRR 145
marked a substantial and unprecedented shift from the large load interconnection framework that
had previously applied in the ERCOT region.

        Under the legacy Large Load Interconnection Study ("LLIS") process, large load
interconnection requests proceeded individually through a TSP-led process. The TSP scheduled
the kickoff meeting with the ILLE and ERCOT, developed the study scope, conducted or
coordinated steady-state, short-circuit, and stability analyses, and communicated results and next
steps to the ILLE.1 The Batch Zero process upended that framework entirely.

        The scope and speed of this transformation cannot be overstated. An entity that had been
proceeding through the legacy interconnection process was suddenly required to comply with an
entirely new set of requirements within a matter of weeks, or face exclusion from any
interconnection path and achieve energization for many years in the future.

        Critically, the Batch Zero process was designed primarily in response to the surge in data
center interconnection requests, not to address the impacts of industrial manufacturing loads like
Synergen' s Proj ect. Data centers and industrial plants operate on fundamentally different
development timelines and decision-making cycles. A data center developer may be able to
identify a site, secure land, and commit to an interconnection timeline in a matter of months. An
industrial green ammonia plant, by contrast, requires years of permitting, environmental review,
engineering design, procurement of highly specialized and long-lead-time equipment (such as -

1 See Planning Guide §§ 9.8.2,9.8.3.


                                                  3
 hydrogen electrolyzers, Haber Bosch reactors, high voltage high load power transformers, and
manufacture of processing equipment modules), and phased construction before it can begin
operations. The Batch Zero process swept industrial loads, like Synergen's, into the same
framework as data centers without adequate consideration of these critical differences in
development timelines, capital raise and deployment schedules, and operational complexity.

         ERCOT itself has acknowledged the challenges created by the compressed implementation
timeline. In its August 10, 2026 filing with the Commission, ERCOT stated that "PGRR 145 was
adopted and implemented on a compressed timeline. As a result, not all ILLEs were able to
demonstrate strict compliance with all applicable eligibility criteria."2 ERCOT further reported
that it receivedfbrty-one good cause exception requests from ILLEs - a number that, standing
alone, demonstrates the breadth of the compliance challenges created by the rapid implementation
of an entirely new process.3

        Synergen, as a green ammonia manufacturer with no prior experience navigating ERCOT' s
large load interconnection processes, had no reasonable basis to anticipate the adoption and rapid
retroactive implementation of a system-wide batch interconnection process that would impose hard
deadlines applicable to its Proj ect. The prior framework gave no notice that such a process was
forthcoming, and the twenty-two-day window between approval and the first deadline was wholly
insufficient for an entity in Synergen' s position to identify, understand, and comply with the new
requirements.

        As an industrial end-use customer and first-time participant in ERCOT's large load
interconnection process, Synergen reasonably relied upon STEC, as its Interconnecting TSP, to
guide Synergen through the requisite steps to achieve interconnection and energization. This
reliance was both reasonable and consistent with the structure of the interconnection framework
itself.

        Under the legacy LLIS process, the TSP played a central role in managing and facilitating
the interconnection study process on behalf ofthe ILLE. Even under the new Batch Zero process,
the TSP remains the entity responsible for submitting eligibility information, attestations, financial
security confirmations, and required disclosures to ERCOT on the ILLE' s behalf.4 The entire
architecture of the interconnection process - both legacy and current - is built around the TSP
as the primary interface between the ILLE and ERCOT.

       This reliance was borne out in the parties' actual course of dealing. Synergen initiated
contact with STEC regarding this Project as early as July 2024 and executed a non-disclosure
agreement with STEC that same month. Synergen confirmed its point of interconnection,

2 See Review of ERCOT 's Interconnection Process for Large Loads, Project No . 59142 , Electric Reliability Council
of Texas, Inc.'s Requests for Good Cause Exceptions to Batch Zero Deadlines and Status Update on Additional
Matters Including the Long-Term Load Forecast. (Aug. 10, 2026).
3 Id.
4 See Planning Guide § 9.3.1(2)(a).


                                                        4
 submitted a request for proposal for substation construction, and formally contracted with STEC
to perform a Load Study and ERCOT System Impact Study ("SIS") in August 2025; STEC
invoiced Synergen $200,000 for those studies the following month, which the parties understood
to be conclusive engineering services - that is, a definitive determination of whether, and how,
the interconnecting transmission system could be upgraded to deliver the Project's requested load.
STEC completed a Steady State Report on April 24,2026. It was not until a July 7,2026 discussion
- 3 days before the July 10, 2026 dynamic-data submission deadline became effective - that
STEC and Synergen discussed PGRR 145 in any detail, at which time Synergen confirmed that it
could not provide the financial security within the time frame required to participate in Batch Zero.
The result of these rapid changes which seemingly moved at an arbitrary pace is that Synergen
was unduly left out of the Batch Zero process.

   B. Synergen's $30.5 Million Substantial Investment to Date

        Synergen has invested approximately $30.5 million in the Project, including expenditures
on permitting, environmental compliance, engineering and design, procurement of specialized
industrial equipment, site preparation and securing commitments from offtakers to purchase the
finished product /ammonia, and securing commitments from lenders and investors to provide the
capital for construction. Development work and capital expenditure on the proj ect has been
ongoing continuously over the past 18 months. The investment to date of approximately $30.5
million is substantial, irreversible, and made in reasonable reliance on the regulatory and
interconnection framework then in effect.

        Synergen understands the rationale behind PGRR-145 is to identify projects and loads at
an advanced stage of development, and with a high probability of receiving proj ect finance and
achieving commercial operation. Synergen understands that the security deposit requirement was
one tool to filter serious/real projects from conceptual projects. While a multi-million-dollar
security instrument for load posted by a large corporation (typically for energy or data projects
only) at a far earlier stage of the development cycle will separate those who can post the security
from those who cannot it does not increase the probability that the proj ect will overcome other
development challenges and achieve Commercial Operation. However, using a tool like financial
security to effectively gate keep access to energization discriminates against traditional
developers that followed the conventional and proven project development path for a diverse
range of projects that are essential/needed outside energy and data projects.

         Additionally, the retroactive application of the financial security criteria kills this type of
proj ect, wastes millions of dollars already invested, harms (perhaps irreparably) the conventional
developer, and squanders the opportunity for jobs and tax revenues needed by communities to
maintain and grow their infrastructure to provide a pathway to prosperity for future generations.

Synergen's project is a 300MW load which, at $50,000/MW, translates into a $15,000,000 security
under the new regulations . Consider that Synergen has already spent over $ 30 , 000 , 000 which


                                                   5
 translates into an investment of over $100,000/MW - double the required security. Additionally,
Synergen has agreements, condition precedent upon Synergen securing the load and GIA, for
construction capital and product offtake.

Based on these achievements, acquired under the conventional development path, Synergen
requests:

          i)      an exception (by an extension) to the deadline for posting the required financial
                  security until the nearly completed load study is finalized and project' s FID
                  achieved.5

          ii)     Inclusion in Batch Zero, because the Steady State portion of the load study was
                  completed in April 2026 and the system upgrade/energization timeline of Q1 2028
                  was given by STEC. Finalization of the remaining part of study is imminent.

          The Project represents a significant commitment to Texas's industrial base and the state' s
clean energy economy. Green ammonia production is a critical component of the global effort to
decarbonize agriculture (by complimenting fossil-fuel-derived ammonia fertilizer in times of
global events or extreme shortages), shipping (as a zero-carbon maritime fuel), and energy storage
(as a hydrogen carrier). The Project is precisely the type of industrial development that Texas' s
energy and economic policies should be encouraging - a capital-intensive, j ob-creating
manufacturing facility that leverages the state's abundant energy resources to produce a globally
demanded industrial product.

        Exclusion from Batch Zero would cause severe and irreversible harm to the Proj ect. Under
Planning Guide § 9.2.1(4), a large load that does not meet the Batch Zero eligibility criteria "shall
be ineligible to receive approval for Initial Energization until evaluated through a future
interconnection study process." No such future process has been defined, and no timeline for one
has been established. The Project cannot survive such a delay in interconnection and energization.
Synergen' s financing, contractual commitments, and business plan are predicated on achieving
energization within a commercially reasonable timeframe. An indefinite hold would result in the
Project's financial failure, the loss of approximately $30.5 million already invested, and the
forfeiture of the jobs, tax revenue, and economic development the Project would bring to the
region.

        The harm to Synergen is disproportionate to any interest served by strict enforcement of
deadlines that Synergen, through no fault of its own, did not know applied to its Proj ect. The
equities overwhelmingly favor granting the requested exception.




5 The posting of the security alone does not trigger any expenditure by the TSP or create a power price increase for
ratepayers)


                                                         6
    C. Flexible Load Profile + Self-Generation: Further Strengthening the Grid
        Beyond the equities specific to Synergen, granting the requested exception serves the
public interest because the Project is designed in ways that reduce, rather than exacerbate, its
impact on ERCOT system reliability.

        Due to the technology and operating controls built into Synergen's plant the load profile
can be very flexible compared to other conventional large industrial loads. Additionally, Synergen
will bring approximately 890 MW of owned and contracted renewable generation to the Proj ect,
including a 290 MW behind-the-meter solar facility and approximately 600 MW of wind
generation procured under long-term power purchase agreements - an approach consistent with
the "bring-your-own-generation" model that ERCOT has separately recognized as improving
resource adequacy and reducing reliance on transmission capacity.

         At a time when the Commission and ERCOT are managing an unprecedented surge in
large-load interconnection requests and the resulting strain on system reliability, the Project
represents precisely the type of self-supplied, curtailable industrial load that PGRR 145 and related
initiatives are designed to encourage. Granting the requested exception would not undermine those
goals; it would advance them.

   D. Financial Security Posting: Request for Time Extension

       Conventional industrial projects follow a different financing path of non-recourse project
financing which is typically not available until Final Investment Decision ("FID") and occurs only
after permitting, offtake arrangements, and interconnection certainties are substantially finalized.
Requiring an industrial developer to post multi-million dollar security before FID discriminates
and imposes a structural barrier that has little to do with whether the underlying project is real,
viable, or ready to proceed.

       Synergen currently has many investor discussions at an advanced stage, with one term
sheet of $80 Million, with power confirmation being a condition precedent. Hence, Synergen
humbly requests an extension for posting the financial security following the completion of the
Batch Zero load study.


                                        III.    CONCLUSION
        Synergen respectfully requests that the Commission grant the requested good cause
exception and direct ERCOT to include the Proj ect in the Batch Zero process notwithstanding
Synergen' s failure to meet the July 10 and July 24, 2026 eligibility deadlines, permit ERCOT to
provisionally treat the applicable eligibility deadlines as satisfied while this request is pending,
permit Synergen to satisfy any Batch Zero financial security requirement through a security deposit
structured as a condition precedent to Batch Zero inclusion, to be posted upon (i) confirmation of



                                                 7
 the Project' s inclusion in Batch Zero and (ii) Synergen' s procurement of commitments for its full
requested load, and grant such other and further relief as the Commission deems just and proper.

       In summary:

       •   Synergen' s Project is a non-computational load requiring 300 MW demand capacity;

       •   The Proj ect will have 890 MW (290 MW of solar behind the meter and 600 MW of
           wind from Texas region) of generation that can contribute to the "Bring your own
           Generation" concept;

       •   Synergen' s flexible load profile enhances ERCOT' s grid reliability objectives;

       •   The Project was unable to submit Batch Zero materials due to the harsh timing ofPGRR
           145;

       •   However, Synergen has invested $30.5 Million ($100,000/MW) into project
           development through engineering studies, environmental assessments, water
           assessment, site preparation, etc. Hence, the company' s investment to date outweighs
           the security required by a factor of 2; and

       •   Synergen' s proj ect brings much needed investment into Calhoun County, including 60
           high paying full-time jobs and 150+ construction jobs during peak construction
           activity, and new tax revenues necessary to sustain the rural area.

Therefore, Synergen humbly requests inclusion in Batch Zero via a good cause exception to 1.
extend the deadline for the financial security upon completion of the Batch Zero load study; and
2. extend the deadline for the completion of required studies.




                                      Respectfully submitted,



                                      l s/ Pranav Tanti

                                      Pranav Tanti
                                      CEO & President
                                      Synergen Green Energy, Inc.




                                                 8

FORMAL LETTER OF OPPOSITION

REQUEST TO DENY SYNERGEN GREEN ENERGY INC.'S GOOD CAUSE EXCEPTION

November 17, 2026

To: Public Utility Commission of Texas
Cc: Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT)
Re: PUCT Project No. 59142 – Item No. 57

Dear Commissioners:

I am writing as a Calhoun County homeowner, agricultural landowner, and concerned
resident to formally oppose Synergen Green Energy Inc.'s request for a Good Cause
Exception to ERCOT's Batch Zero eligibility requirements.

I respectfully but firmly request that the Commission DENY Synergen's request in its
entirety.

After reviewing Synergen's request and the letter circulated by John Hewitt soliciting support
for the exception, I am particularly concerned by the attempt to frame this matter as a choice
between economic development and a small group of residents supposedly standing in the
way of Calhoun County's future.

That is a false choice.

We are not against economic development. We are against the expectation that residents
should accept a major industrial project, overlook unanswered questions, and support
special regulatory treatment simply because a developer promises jobs and tax revenue.

1. Synergen's failure to meet requirements is the company's responsibility.

Mr. Hewitt argues that the new Batch Zero requirements were sudden, stringent, and
designed primarily for large corporations and hyperscalers.

However, the requirements apply to developers seeking to participate in the process. A
company choosing to pursue a project of this magnitude has a responsibility to understand
regulatory requirements, plan accordingly, and meet established deadlines.

ERCOT's published implementation activities began before the July submission deadlines.
The argument that Synergen had only a few days to prepare does not, by itself, establish good
cause.

The Commission should examine the actual timeline, the information made available to
applicants, and Synergen's own preparation efforts.
 A company's failure to meet a deadline should not automatically become grounds for
special treatment.

2. Synergen's $30.5 million investment does not entitle it to an exception.

Synergen repeatedly emphasizes its approximately $30.5 million investment and its
proposed $550 million-plus project.

That investment represents a private business decision. It does not create a financial
obligation for Calhoun County residents, ERCOT, or the State of Texas.

Nor should it give Synergen an advantage over other developers that complied with the
established requirements.

If a company can miss deadlines and then argue that its investment is too large to lose, the
regulatory process becomes unequal. The more money a developer spends, the more
pressure it can place on regulators to grant an exception.

That is not a sound basis for public policy.

A private investment is not a regulatory entitlement.

3. The missing payment security is a serious concern.

Synergen acknowledges that it did not provide the required payment security by the
applicable deadline.

This is not simply an overlooked piece of paperwork. Financial security is an important part
of the eligibility process for large electrical loads.

The Commission should not dismiss this requirement because Synergen has already spent
millions of dollars.

If financial security is required, it should be provided. If a developer cannot satisfy the
requirement, the Commission should not assume the financial risk or weaken the standard
to accommodate that developer.

Other applicants should not be disadvantaged because they fulfilled obligations that
Synergen failed to meet.

4. The claim of 300 MW of new electricity generation requires independent verification.

Synergen's support letter promotes the claim that the project will add approximately 300 MW
of clean power generation to ERCOT.
 Yet the project description identifies a 240 MW hydrogen electrolyzer, approximately 290 MW
of on-site solar generation, and approximately 600 MW of contracted Texas wind power.

These figures raise important questions about the project's actual electricity requirements
and its contribution to the grid.

How much electricity will the facility consume? How much new generation will actually be
constructed? How much electricity will be delivered to ERCOT? Will the facility draw
electricity from the grid when its renewable sources are unavailable?

Contracted renewable power is not automatically the same as new generation physically
added to the grid.

The Commission should require independently verifiable engineering documentation before
accepting the claim that this project will provide approximately 300 MW of additional
generation.

The actual electrical demand and grid impact of the facility must be evaluated, not simply
its promotional description.

5. Economic projections are not guaranteed benefits to Calhoun County.

The support letter cites more than $974 million in regional economic impact, $255 million in
direct wages, and $171 million in local tax revenue over 35 years.

These figures are projections, not guaranteed payments.

The same applies to the promised 60 permanent jobs and 150 peak construction jobs.

How many of those jobs will actually go to Calhoun County residents? What portions of the
projected tax revenue will reach our local taxing entities? What happens if the project is
delayed, reduced, or fails to operate as anticipated?

A private economic impact study should not be treated as proof that these benefits will
materialize.

Calhoun County deserves realistic expectations and enforceable commitments, not
impressive projections used to persuade regulators to overlook missed requirements.

6. Synergen does not speak for all of Calhoun County.

I strongly object to Mr. Hewitt's characterization of project opponents as a "small but well-
organized minority."

That description is dismissive of residents who have legitimate concerns about their homes,
land, groundwater, air quality, wildlife, and future generations.
 The number of people who support or oppose a project does not determine whether it meets
regulatory requirements.

Nor does a company's history of meeting with local officials, organizations, and economic
development groups establish unanimous community support.

There are residents throughout Calhoun County who believe this project presents significant
questions that have not been adequately answered.

We should not be labeled obstructionists simply because we expect transparency and
accountability.

Calhoun County is not merely a location on a developer's investment map. It is our
home.

Our water, land, air, natural resources, and quality of life have value beyond the projected
financial return of one industrial project.

7. Calling this project green does not eliminate its environmental responsibilities.

Synergen describes its proposed ammonia facility as environmentally clean.

That description does not eliminate the need for independent review of its water
consumption, electricity requirements, industrial emissions, chemical handling, safety
plans, and environmental impacts.

Our county is a peninsula with groundwater resources that are especially important to the
people who live and own property here.

Residents should not be expected to accept additional industrial demands on our natural
resources without complete and transparent information.

The fact that a project produces green ammonia does not automatically make every aspect
of its operation environmentally harmless.

Economic promises should never replace environmental accountability.

8. The Commission must not establish a precedent of preferential treatment.

The most troubling argument in the support letter is that Synergen deserves an exception
because the company has invested substantial money and because the community
supposedly needs the economic benefits.

That is not the standard by which regulatory decisions should be made.
 The PUCT must evaluate the request based on the applicable rules, the evidence presented,
and the public interest.

If a developer can receive special treatment because it has already spent millions of dollars,
other developers that met their obligations are placed at a disadvantage.

The Commission must protect the integrity of the Batch Zero process.

Rules that apply to everyone should not become negotiable for a company that has
failed to comply.

FORMAL REQUEST

I respectfully request that the Public Utility Commission of Texas:

   1. DENY Synergen Green Energy Inc.'s Good Cause Exception request in its entirety.

   2. Refuse to waive or excuse the applicable Batch Zero eligibility requirements based
      solely on the company's financial investment or projected economic benefits.

   3. Evaluate the company's failure to provide the required load study and payment
      security against the actual eligibility standards and the evidence submitted.

   4. Protect the consistent and equal application of ERCOT's requirements for all
      developers.

   5. Give appropriate consideration to the technical, financial, and public-interest
      concerns raised by residents who have submitted opposition.

I want to be very clear: Calhoun County needs economic opportunities. We need good jobs
and responsible businesses. But we do not need to sacrifice fairness, accountability, or the
interests of our residents to accommodate one company's business plans.

Mr. Hewitt suggests that those opposing this project could be responsible for depriving
Calhoun County of its future.

I reject that suggestion.

The responsibility for meeting regulatory requirements belongs to the company
proposing the project. It does not belong to the residents who are asking legitimate
questions and exercising their right to participate in the regulatory process.

A company's investment does not guarantee approval. Projected tax revenue does not
excuse noncompliance. And the promise of jobs does not give any developer the right to
special treatment.
 The PUCT has a responsibility to all Texans, not simply to the financial interests of one private
developer.

I urge the Commission to uphold its requirements, protect the integrity of the regulatory
process, and DENY SYNERGEN'S REQUEST FOR A GOOD CAUSE EXCEPTION.

Respectfully submitted,



Name: _Annie Flores

Calhoun County, Texas

Date: November 17, 2026
 

=== Hewitt Synergen Letter re PUC trying to gather support.pdf ===
From: Elizabeth Sherry <Elizabeth.Sherry@SynergenGreen.com>
Sent: Tuesday, November 17, 2026 11:23 AM
To: Elizabeth Sherry <Elizabeth.Sherry@SynergenGreen.com>
Subject: Letter of Support

CAUTION: External Email: Be Cyber-Alert

This email is to request you provide a Letter of Support for our project to help keep our
project alive. It is a long email, but we ask that you read it in its entirety, as it explains
the reasons for our request and, we hope, convinces you that your Letter is a worthy
cause and will make a di erence.

Dear Supporter

 As you may be aware, the recent and sudden projected growth in data centers brought with
it new and enormous demands for electric power. These demands are labelled as
“Computational Loads” and the large corporations driving the growth characterized as
“Hyperscalers”. These demands far exceeded the existing strategic plans for new power
generation in every Regional Transmission Organization (RTOs) across the nation, including
ERCOT. The Federal Government, via FERC and the DoE issued directives to the RTOs to
accommodate this new demand.

 ERCOTs response was to change the way in which applications for new loads are
processed. Until July 2026 new load applications were accepted and studied, by local
transmission and distribution organizations (T&D) on a case-by-case basis as applications
were made. This process has been upended and ERCOT now clubs applications together
into Batches, beginning with “Batch Zero,” and performs the studies itself. The new rules
are still evolving and the expected timeline for the batch process is still uncertain.

 The change to the Batch Process was sudden and brought with it stringent new
commercial demands in order to qualify for the Batch process, including requirements for
applicants to post signiﬁcant ﬁnancial deposits to securitize the load. These deposits were
intended to act as a ﬁlter to determine which of the load applications were real and which
were not, and as the requirements were intended for large corporations/hyperscalers they
are stringent and onerous. Unfortunately, the new requirements are a “one size ﬁts all”
requirement which has the e ect of excluding, and therefore discriminating, against
traditional project developers, especially those small to medium business that are not part
of a large corporation. The impact of the change is that many projects that have been under
development for several years and have already invested large sums of money fall short of
 the new requirements and real projects are at risk of being “thrown out with the trash”

center interconnection requests, not to address the impacts of industrial manufacturing loads like

development timelines and decision-making cycles. A data center developer may be able to
identify a site, secure land, and commit to an interconnection timeline in a matter of months. An

Asyou may be aware, the recent and sudden projected growth in data centers brought with
it new and enormous demands for electric power. These demands are labelled as
"Computational Loads" and the large corporations drivingthe growth characterized as
"Hyperscalers". These demands far exceeded the existing strategic plans for new power
generation in every Regional Transmission Organization (RTOs) across the nation, including
ERCOT. The Federal Government, via FERC and the DoE issued directives to the RTOs to
accom modate this new demand.

ERCOTs response was to change the way in which applications for new loads are
processed. Until July 2026 new load applications were accepted and studied, by local
transmission and distribution organizations (T&D) on a case-by-case basis as applications
were made. This process has been upended and ERCOT now clubs applicationstogether
into Batches, beginning with "Batch Zero," and performs the studies itself. The new rules
are still evolving and the expected timeline for the batch process is still uncertain.

The change to the Batch Process was sudden and brought with it stringent new
commercial demands in orderto qualify forthe Batch process, including requirements for
applicants to post significant financial deposits to securitize the load. These deposits were
intended to act as a filterto determine which of the load applications were real and which
were not, and as the requirements were intended for large corporations/hyperscalers they
are stringent and onerous. Unfortunately, the new requirements are a "one size fits all"
requirement which has the effect of excluding, and therefore discriminating, against
traditional project developers, especially those smallto medium business thatare not part
of a large corporation. The impact of the change is that many projects that have been under
development for severalyears and have already invested large sums of money fall short of
 the new requirements and real projects are at risk of being"thrown out with the trash"
wasting all the efforts and resources spent to date and depriving communities of the
benefits and opportunities they had been expectingand planning for.

Fortunately, the Public Utility Commission of Texas (PUCT) and ERCOT, have established a
"Good Cause Exception" process bywhich project developers, like Synergen can plead
their case for inclusion in the Batch process, although many, if not all, of the qualification
criteria remain the same. Synergen has alreadysubmitted a Good Cause Exception letter
to the PUCT/ERCOT and the ruling is expected in early December.

As is normal, not everyone supports our project, and there is a small but well-organized
minority who actively oppose the project. The opposition is mainly localto the project
location and chose to overlook the benefits to the county as a whole. It has come to our
notice that people opposed to the project have written to the PUCT / ERCOT requestingthat
they reject Synergen's Good Cause Exception request on the grounds that the
responsibilityto meet regulatory requirements belongs tothe companyproposingthe
project, not the community where it intends to operate.

If the project opponents are successful in their endeavors to delay the project, the project
